brief: GS's EMEA desk ties Wednesday's violent US equity liquidation to new BIS chip-export rules (effective Nov 19, closing the offshore-compute loophole), which compound existing AI-multiple concerns: cost of capital (worsened by NVDA's leadership change), data-center restrictions, inference oversupply, and a capex-revenue mismatch. Technical support broke, breadth collapsed (38 advancers vs 464 decliners), and defensive sectors lost absolute protection. Hawkish Fed commentary (Waller's 50bp remarks) tightened financial conditions sharply, collapsing breakevens against real yields; the desk flags 2018-style overtightening risk and a possible shift from an inflation to a growth/liquidity problem, favors receiving rates, and reads extreme de-grossing as a possible tactical local low, with November CPI the next catalyst. Regionally, Asia-Pacific was net sold $2bn, led by China/HK/Korea selling, while Japan and Taiwan saw inflows; hedge funds de-grossed broadly and AI/tech exporters sold hard across China, Taiwan, Korea and Japan even as China's domestic AI hardware held up. India bucked the trend (record FII inflows, GS's Overweight upgrade) while Korea's AI-driven selloff pushed GS to cut its KOSPI target to 7,500. GS's 2027 outlook raises China H and India to Overweight, cuts Taiwan and China A to Marketweight.

cards.claim: New BIS export rules, effective November 19 and directed by Treasury and the NSC, represent a significant tightening of the US chip export regime.
cards.anchor: The new BIS rules, effective November 19 and directed by Treasury and the NSC, represent a pretty sizeable intervention.

cards.claim: The new export rules tighten restrictions on both direct chip sales to China and on advanced compute accessed remotely by Chinese entities through overseas data centers.
cards.anchor: The rules tighten restrictions not just on direct chip sales to China, but also on specified advanced compute accessed remotely by Chinese entities through overseas data centers.

cards.claim: The new rules are effectively an attempt to close the offshore compute loophole, overlapping substantially with the proposed RASA legislation.
cards.anchor: Effectively an attempt to close the offshore compute loophole, with substantial overlap with the proposed RASA legislation.

cards.claim: China now faces pressure on three fronts: direct chip access, remote access to overseas compute, and its ability to manufacture leading-edge technology via tighter foundry restrictions.
cards.anchor: China now faces pressure on three fronts: direct access to advanced chips, remote access to overseas compute and its ability to manufacture leading edge technology, with tighter restrictions on overseas foundries.

cards.claim: The desk views the immediate issue as licensing-regime uncertainty, potentially enough to freeze incremental AI investment, rather than permanent loss of Chinese chip demand.
cards.anchor: Think the most immediate issue isn’t the permanent loss of Chinese demand, but the uncertainty over who can access what, and under which licensing regime.

cards.claim: The desk partially attributes acute weakness in the Asian data center trade to the new rules, alongside broader China weakness with the Shanghai market testing its lows.
cards.anchor: I think this partially explains why the Asian data center trade has been so acutely weak, alongside broader China weakness and the Shanghai market testing its lows.

cards.claim: The desk sees potential knock-on effects from the AI/chip stress into copper and gold prices, though broader liquidity and positioning are also at work.
cards.anchor: Potential knock  on effects into copper and gold, although broader liquidity and positioning are clearly also at work.

cards.claim: Four structural concerns are cited as having driven AI-related equity multiples down: cost of capital, data center restrictions, oversupply/efficiency unlocks for inference, and lack of revenue to support capex.
